pos: n. (town of Vastergotland; the oldest Swedish bishopric, founded about 1014)
etymology: From Old Swedish Skara, probably from a word for a cut or notch in the land.
biblical_def: Skara holds the oldest see in Sweden, founded about 1014 under the first Christian kings, five centuries before the Reformation reached it. Its last Roman bishop, Magnus Haraldsson, took part in the Vastergotland rising of 1529 against Gustav Vasa, in which disaffected nobles made common cause with peasants who wanted the old religion back; the rising collapsed, and the bishop fled the country. The diocese was then given evangelical superintendents and its cathedral school continued. The dictionary records Skara because the oldest foundation in a country is where the question of foundations is most naturally raised, and Scripture is emphatic that the church has only one. Paul will not build where another has laid a foundation, “lest I should build upon another man's foundation” (Rom 15:20), and when he does lay one he warns everyone who builds after him to be careful what he puts on it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a foundation as the basis of an edifice, that on which anything stands; a corner stone as the stone which lies at the corner of two walls and unites them; and a masterbuilder as a chief builder, an architect.
webster_full: FOUNDATION, n. [L. fundatio.] The basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground; the basis or groundwork of anything.
CORNER-STONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone, and especially the stone which forms the corner of the foundation.
MASTERBUILDER, n. A chief builder; an architect; one who directs the work of others.
TRIED, participle passive. Proved; examined; settled; having stood the test.
scriptures: Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation:
According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon.
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.
Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
corruption_summary: Sweden's oldest bishopric, from about 1014; its last Roman bishop joined the 1529 rising and fled the country.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the appeal to antiquity as a foundation in itself, which is Rome's standing argument and the one most often made against the Reformation: a see of five hundred years must be right because it is old. Age proves continuity, not truth. Skara was five centuries old and had to be reformed, and the reforming was a return to something older still.

The principle to recover is that the foundation is laid once, by God, and consists of the apostolic and prophetic word with Christ as its corner. Isaiah announces the laying of it: “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation” (Isa 28:16). Paul says the church is “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20). And every builder after that is on notice: “let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon” (1Co 3:10).

pos: n. (cathedral city of Ostergotland, Sweden; see of Hans Brask, the last Catholic bishop, whose hidden reservation gave Swedish a proverb)
etymology: From Swedish Linköping, the market by the lime trees or by the Lin stream; köping, a market town.
biblical_def: Linkoping was the richest Swedish diocese and the see of Hans Brask, the last Roman Catholic bishop in Sweden to hold his post, an energetic administrator who founded the country's first printing press in 1523 and used it against Luther. In 1517 he was compelled to set his seal to the deposition of Archbishop Trolle, and afterwards produced a small slip of paper he had hidden under the seal reading that he was forced and consented not. The Swedish language has kept the word brasklapp for a concealed reservation ever since. Brask fled Sweden in 1527 after the Diet of Vasteras and died in a Polish monastery. The dictionary records the city because the brasklapp is a perfect specimen of a sin Scripture treats with unusual severity, the oath taken with a private escape clause. Christ forbids the whole apparatus in a sentence: “But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Mat 5:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a reservation as the act of keeping back, something withheld; an oath as a solemn affirmation with an appeal to God for its truth; and to contemn as to despise, to slight, to neglect.
webster_full: RESERVATION, n. The act of reserving or keeping back; concealment or withholding from disclosure; something withheld, either not expressed or disclosed.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
CONTEMN, v.t. [L. contemno.] To despise; to consider and treat as mean and despicable; to reject with disdain.
EQUIVOCATE, v.i. [L. aequivocus.] To use words of a doubtful signification; to express one's opinions in terms which admit of different senses.
scriptures: Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Jam 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
Psa 15:4
In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
corruption_summary: The richest Swedish see; Bishop Hans Brask's hidden slip disclaiming his own sealed signature gave Swedish the word brasklapp.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is mental reservation, which late medieval moral theology developed into a system and which Rome's casuists defended at length: a man may use words in a sense his hearer will not take, or sign with a secret intention that voids the signing, and so keep his conscience while deceiving his neighbour. Brask was under real duress and the dictionary does not equate his slip with the worst of the casuists; but the device is the same device, and it corrupts speech at the root by making every assurance conditional on something the hearer cannot see.

The principle to recover is that the Christian's word stands without machinery. James repeats his Lord's command and adds the sanction: “let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation” (Jam 5:12). The psalm marks out the man who may dwell in God's hill as one who keeps a promise that has turned out badly for him, “He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” (Psa 15:4). And Proverbs sets the two kinds of speech against each other without a middle term: “Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight” (Pro 12:22).

pos: n. (oldest surviving town in Sweden, founded about 980; an early Christian centre long decayed by the Reformation)
etymology: From Old Norse Sigtuna, probably the enclosure by the water; tun, an enclosed place.
biblical_def: Sigtuna was the first town of Christian Sweden. Founded about 980 on Lake Malaren, it had the earliest Swedish mint, the first stone churches, and for a time the kingdom's chief market; it was burned by raiders in 1187 and never recovered its trade, and by the Reformation it was a small place among ruins, with four or five roofless churches standing in a town of a few hundred people. Its Dominican priory was dissolved in the 1530s. The dictionary records Sigtuna because the ruins of an early Christian foundation standing in a reformed country are an unusually plain figure of what the Reformation understood itself to be doing. It did not think it was building a new religion; it thought it was repairing an old one. Isaiah's promise is the Reformation's own self-description: “they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places” (Isa 58:12), and the name given to such men is the repairer of the breach.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a breach as a gap, an opening made by breaking; to repair as to restore to a sound state after decay; and waste as desolate, destroyed, uncultivated.
webster_full: BREACH, n. The act of breaking; a gap or opening made by breaking; the violation of a law or covenant.
REPAIR, v.t. [L. reparo.] To restore to a sound state after decay or injury; to rebuild a part decayed or lost.
WASTE, adj. Destroyed; ruined; desolate; uncultivated; unoccupied; lying unused.
RESTORE, v.t. [L. restauro.] To return to a former state; to repair; to bring back to its former condition.
scriptures: And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
Neh 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
Amo 9:11
In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old:
Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
corruption_summary: Sweden's oldest town, Christian from about 980, a place of roofless churches and a few hundred people by the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error nearer at hand is the one both sides of the sixteenth century made about the other: Rome calling the Reformation an innovation, and radicals treating it as a fresh start owing nothing to the fifteen centuries before it. The Reformers claimed neither. They claimed to be clearing rubble off a foundation that was already there.

The principle to recover is that God's way with a ruined church is repair, and that He summons men to the work rather than doing it over their heads. Nehemiah stated the case to the people before a stone was lifted: “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17). Amos promises the raising of what has fallen, “and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old” (Amo 9:11). And Haggai puts the shaming question to men comfortable among ruins: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4).

pos: n. (town on Lake Vattern, Sweden; the abbey of Birgitta and mother house of the Bridgettine order, dissolved by stages to 1595)
etymology: From Swedish Vadstena, the ford-stone; vad, a ford, and sten, a stone.
biblical_def: Vadstena held the greatest monastic house in the North. Founded on the rule given in the revelations of Birgitta Birgersdotter, who died in Rome in 1373 and was canonised in 1391, it was a double house of nuns and brothers under an abbess, the mother convent of the Bridgettine order, a centre of manuscript production and the chief pilgrimage goal in Sweden. The Reformation did not destroy it at a stroke. The brothers were dispersed in the 1540s, the nuns were forbidden to receive novices, and the last of them left in 1595, after which the buildings became a hospital and an asylum. The dictionary records Vadstena because the two corruptions it rested on are both named in Scripture and both still live: a rule of life drawn from private revelation, and a holiness measured by abstinence. Paul names the first exactly: a man “intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind” (Col 2:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vow as a solemn promise made to God; an abbey as a monastery or society of persons secluded from the world and devoted to religion; and will worship as worship of one's own devising.
webster_full: VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity; a solemn promise accompanied by an appeal to God.
ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion.
CLOISTER, n. [L. claustrum.] A monastery or nunnery; a house inhabited by monks or nuns.
REVELATION, n. The act of disclosing or discovering to others what was before unknown to them; that which is revealed by God to man.
scriptures: Col 2:18
Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
corruption_summary: The North's greatest abbey, founded on Birgitta's revelations; brothers dispersed in the 1540s, the last nuns gone by 1595.
corruption_paragraphs: Three corruptions met at Vadstena and the dictionary names each. First, private revelation treated as a rule binding consciences: Birgitta's visions, whatever her sincerity, were not Scripture and could not found an order. Second, the monastic vow itself, which imposes as a higher calling a celibacy and poverty God has not required, and so divides the church into two grades of Christian. Third, the pilgrimage and the cult of a canonised saint, which Rome maintains to this day and has not withdrawn.

The principle to recover is that worship and the rule of life come from the commandment of God and not from the devising of men. Paul grants that such regimes look impressive and denies that they achieve anything, since they “have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body” (Col 2:23). He lists the marks of the apostasy he foresaw, “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” (1Ti 4:3). And Christ pronounces the whole class of such devotions void: “But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9).

pos: n. (cathedral city of Smaland, Sweden; the diocese from which the Dacke rising of 1542 drew its strength)
etymology: From Swedish Växjö, probably the lake by the road; väg, road, and sjö, lake.
biblical_def: Vaxjo is the see of Smaland, the forested southern province whose people rose against Gustav Vasa in 1542 under Nils Dacke. The Dacke rising was the most dangerous rebellion of the reign: it was provoked by taxation, by the crown's trade restrictions and by the seizure of church goods, and it demanded the restoration of the old religion along with the old liberties, the rebels reopening churches to the Latin mass in the territory they held. It was crushed in 1543 and Dacke was killed. The dictionary records the diocese because the rising poses the hardest question the Reformation century asked of ordinary Christians: whether a people may take up arms to recover a religion their king has taken away. Scripture answers that they may not, and it gives the answer without regard to how unjust the ruler is: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rebellion as an open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government; subjection as the act of subduing, and the state of being under the power of another; and a power as authority, dominion.
webster_full: REBELLION, n. [L. rebellio.] An open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes allegiance.
SUBJECTION, n. The act of subduing; the state of being under the power, control and government of another.
POWER, n. [L. posse.] Command; the right of governing, or actual government; dominion; rule; sway; authority.
ORDINANCE, n. [from ordain.] A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Rom 13:2
Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.
Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme;
Tit 3:1
Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work,
corruption_summary: The Smaland see; the Dacke rising of 1542 demanded the old religion with the old liberties and was crushed the next year.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions stand opposed here and the dictionary rejects both. The first is the rebels': religion recovered by the sword from a lawful magistrate, which is the same error that killed Jon Arason in Iceland and which Scripture forbids regardless of whose religion is the true one. The second is the crown's: a reformation carried through for the sake of the treasury, which gave the rising its grievances and its popular force. A king who strips churches to pay soldiers should not be surprised when the stripped parishes want the old faith back.

The principle to recover is the duty of subjection, with its one limit and no others. Paul states the duty and its sanction: “Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God” (Rom 13:2). Peter adds the motive that makes it bearable under a bad ruler, “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake” (1Pe 2:13). Paul tells Titus to keep the congregation reminded of it, “Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates” (Tit 3:1). The limit is obedience to God where the two commands collide, and it licenses refusal, not revolt.

pos: n. (port of western Sweden, founded 1621; the one place in the Lutheran realm where Reformed worship was legally allowed)
etymology: From Swedish Göteborg, the fortress of the Goths or of the Göta river; borg, a stronghold.
biblical_def: Gothenburg was built to order. Gustavus Adolphus chartered it in 1621 to give Sweden a harbour on the North Sea outside the Danish tolls, laid it out on a Dutch plan with canals, and staffed it with Dutch engineers, merchants and settlers, together with Scots and Germans. Since many of these were Reformed and not Lutheran, their presence was indispensable and their doctrine was illegal, the crown granted them the right to worship in their own congregations; for most of the seventeenth century a Dutch Reformed church and a German congregation stood in the one Swedish city where the Uppsala resolution did not apply. The dictionary records Gothenburg because the arrangement was an accident of commerce that produced something better than its motive: two confessions of the Reformation living side by side without either pretending to be the other. Paul's rule covers the case without erasing the difference: “Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth” (Rom 14:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a congregation as an assembly of persons met for the worship of God; toleration as the allowance of that which is not wholly approved; and a rule as that which is prescribed as a guide to conduct.
webster_full: CONGREGATION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God, and for religious instruction.
TOLERATION, n. The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved; specifically, the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
RULE, n. [L. regula.] That which is prescribed or laid down as a guide to conduct; a determinate mode of action.
CHARTER, n. [L. charta.] A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or privilege.
scriptures: Rom 14:4
Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.
Php 3:16
Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing.
By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. He that loveth not his brother abideth in death.
corruption_summary: Founded 1621 on a Dutch plan; its Reformed settlers were granted their own worship in a realm sworn to the Augsburg Confession.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to avoid in both directions is plain enough. One is the confessional rigour that would rather have no port than a Reformed congregation in it, and which in other states produced expulsions that cost the church some of its best men. The other is the modern indifference that mistakes Gothenburg for an argument that confessions do not matter. The Dutch congregation did not stop being Reformed and the Swedish church did not stop being Lutheran; they simply stopped killing each other over it, which is progress of a real but limited kind.

The principle to recover is that genuine brethren are to be recognised as brethren while the differences between them are still honestly held. Paul tells his readers to walk by the light they have reached, “whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule” (Php 3:16). Christ names the mark by which the world identifies His disciples, and it is not uniformity of judgment: “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another” (Joh 13:35). And John makes that love the evidence of life itself, “because we love the brethren” (1Jo 3:14).

pos: n. (archbishop of Uppsala, 1540–1607; enforced the Uppsala resolution by a visitation so severe that he was deposed for it)
etymology: Latinised Swedish, from Ångermanland, the province of his birth; the given name Hebrew Abraham, father of a multitude.
biblical_def: Abraham Angermannus spent twenty years in exile for refusing King John III's attempt to move the Swedish church back toward Rome, and was made archbishop of Uppsala in 1593 by the assembly that settled the realm's confession. He then set out on a general visitation of southern Sweden in 1596 to enforce it, and enforced it with a rigour that has few parallels: offenders against the moral law were flogged at the church door by his order, nobles were summoned and rebuked, and discipline was applied to persons of every rank without distinction. The nobility complained to Duke Charles, who deposed him in 1599 and kept him imprisoned until his death. The dictionary honours the courage and names the error. Church discipline is commanded, but its measure is restoration and its instrument is not the whip: “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness” (Gal 6:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines discipline as instruction and government, correction, chastisement; to restore as to bring back to a former state; and meekness as softness of temper, mildness, forbearance under injuries.
webster_full: DISCIPLINE, n. [L. disciplina.] Education; instruction and government; subjection to laws and rules; correction; chastisement; punishment intended to correct crimes or errors.
RESTORE, v.t. [L. restauro.] To bring back to a former and better state; to repair; to recover.
MEEKNESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries and provocations.
EDIFICATION, n. Improvement; instruction; the building up of the mind in knowledge and grace.
scriptures: Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many.
So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
For though I should boast somewhat more of our authority, which the Lord hath given us for edification, and not for your destruction, I should not be ashamed:
corruption_summary: Twenty years an exile for refusing a Romeward liturgy, then archbishop; deposed in 1599 for a visitation that flogged offenders at the church door.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions are in view and the dictionary names both. The first is the collapse of discipline altogether, which is the common failing now: a church that will not correct anyone has no visible holiness and no way to protect the Table, and the Reformed confessions treat discipline as a mark of the true church precisely for that reason. The second is Angermannus's: discipline turned into punishment, administered with the magistrate's tools and measured by the severity of the penalty rather than by the recovery of the offender.

The principle to recover is that the end of every censure is the restoring of the man. Paul tells a congregation that a penalty already borne is enough, “Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many” (2Co 2:6), and that the next duty is the opposite of further severity: “ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him” (2Co 2:7), lest he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. He states the limit on his own apostolic authority in the same letter, for it was given “for edification, and not for your destruction” (2Co 10:8).

pos: n. (oldest city of Finland, Swedish Abo; the only Finnish bishopric and the centre of the Finnish Reformation)
etymology: From Finnish Turku, a market place, from an Old East Slavic word for trade; Swedish Åbo, the dwelling by the river.
biblical_def: Turku was the whole of ecclesiastical Finland. The country had one bishopric, founded in the thirteenth century, one cathedral, and one cathedral school, and every Finnish churchman of consequence passed through it. The Reformation came by way of Sweden and by way of men the old bishop had himself sent to Wittenberg; Mikael Agricola, rector of the school and later bishop, printed the first book in Finnish in 1543, an ABC and catechism, followed by a prayer book and in 1548 the Finnish New Testament. Finnish had been a spoken language only; Agricola had to settle its orthography as he went, and the written language dates from his work. The dictionary records Turku because the giving of a written Bible to an unwritten tongue is the clearest form of a promise God makes about language itself: “For then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD” (Zep 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a language as human speech, the expression of ideas by words; a barbarian as a foreigner, one whose speech is not understood; and orthography as the art of writing words with the proper letters.
webster_full: LANGUAGE, n. [L. lingua.] Human speech; the expression of ideas by words or significant articulate sounds.
BARBARIAN, n. [Gr.] A man in his rude, savage state; among the Greeks and Romans, a foreigner; one whose language is not understood.
ORTHOGRAPHY, n. [Gr.] The art of writing words with the proper letters, according to common usage; spelling.
CONSENT, n. [L. consensus.] Agreement of the mind to what is proposed; accord of minds; unity of opinion.
scriptures: Zep 3:9
For then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD, to serve him with one consent.
Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me.
Act 2:6
Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language.
Rev 14:6
And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,
corruption_summary: Finland's only bishopric and the cradle of written Finnish; Agricola printed the first Finnish book in 1543 and the New Testament in 1548.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error nearer at hand is the assumption that a small language is not worth a Bible, which has been made about Finnish, Welsh, Icelandic and several hundred tongues since, and which the missionary translators have refuted every time. A language with no literature received a New Testament and acquired a literature; the Finnish nation's written existence begins with a catechism.

The principle to recover is that God intends to be called upon in every language, and that the preaching reaches a man in his own or does not reach him. Paul states the plain consequence of unintelligibility, that without the meaning of the voice “I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian” (1Co 14:11). At Pentecost the astonishment was exactly this, that “every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6). And John sees the gospel carried to the whole earth by the same measure, “to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” (Rev 14:6).

pos: n. (bishop of Vyborg and then of Turku, c. 1516–1575; wrote the first history of the Finnish church)
etymology: From Finnish-Swedish Juusten, a family name; Latinised Paulus Juusten.
biblical_def: Paul Juusten was Agricola's colleague, rival and successor. Sent like him to Wittenberg, he returned to be rector of the Turku school, became the first bishop of the new see of Vyborg in 1554, and succeeded to Turku itself in 1563. In 1569 John III sent him on an embassy to Russia, where Ivan the Terrible detained the party for three years in conditions of some cruelty; he came home broken and died two years later. His chief book is the Catalogus et ordinaria successio episcoporum Finlandensium, a catalogue of the bishops of Finland from the beginning with an account of each, which is the first Finnish church history and remains a primary source. The dictionary records him because keeping the record of faithful teachers is a duty Scripture lays on the church in plain words: “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God” (Heb 13:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catalogue as a list or enumeration of names set in order; memory as the faculty of the mind by which it retains knowledge, and remembrance; and a successor as one who takes the place another has left.
webster_full: CATALOGUE, n. [Gr.] A list or enumeration of the names of men or things disposed in a certain order, often alphabetical.
MEMORY, n. [L. memoria.] The faculty of the mind by which it retains the knowledge of previous thoughts, impressions or events; also, remembrance.
SUCCESSOR, n. One who succeeds or follows; one who takes the place which another has left, and sustains the like part or character.
CONVERSATION, n. [L. conversatio.] General course of manners; behavior; deportment, especially as it respects morals.
scriptures: Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.
Pro 10:7
The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.
Mal 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
corruption_summary: Bishop of Vyborg and of Turku; three years detained by Ivan the Terrible, and author of the first history of the Finnish church.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the Roman doctrine of apostolic succession, which converts the keeping of such a catalogue into a proof of authority: a chain of consecrations is held to guarantee the doctrine of whoever stands at the end of it. Juusten's own list disproves the claim, since it records bishops of the same see teaching contrary things. The opposite corruption is the modern indifference to a congregation's own history, which leaves each generation with no memory of who taught it and no means of noticing when the teaching changes.

The principle to recover is that the faith of former teachers is to be examined and followed where it was sound, and that God Himself keeps such a record. The psalmist promises that “the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psa 112:6). Proverbs divides the two legacies without sentiment: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot” (Pro 10:7). And Malachi describes the register kept in heaven, where “a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD” (Mal 3:16).

pos: n. (last Roman Catholic bishop of Turku, c. 1480–1550; sent the young Finns to Wittenberg who afterwards reformed his diocese)
etymology: From Swedish Skytte, a marksman or archer; the given name Martin, Latin Martinus.
biblical_def: Martin Skytte was a Dominican, provincial of his order in the North, and from 1528 the last Roman Catholic bishop of Turku. He accepted the Swedish settlement at Vasteras, kept his see for twenty-two years, and made no public break with the old religion; and he also, year after year, chose the ablest boys of his cathedral school and paid to send them to the university at Wittenberg, where Luther and Melanchthon were teaching. Mikael Agricola, Paul Juusten, Thomas Keijoi and others went at his expense and came home evangelical. He received them back, employed them, and let them teach. The dictionary records him because the Finnish Reformation was financed by the man it displaced, and because Scripture is unembarrassed about such things. Joseph's sentence to his brothers covers every case of a purpose overruled: “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (Gen 50:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines providence as the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; a device as that which is formed by design, a scheme or contrivance; and counsel as purpose, design, the plan of God's providence.
webster_full: PROVIDENCE, n. [L. providentia.] The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; a manifestation of the care and direction of God.
DEVICE, n. [Fr. devis.] That which is formed by design; a scheme or contrivance; also, an invention or project.
COUNSEL, n. [L. consilium.] Advice; deliberation; purpose, design; the plan of God's providence.
OVERRULE, v.t. To influence or control by predominant power; to govern with high authority; to supersede.
scriptures: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
Php 1:18
What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.
Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.
corruption_summary: The Dominican bishop who kept his Roman faith and paid to send Agricola and Juusten to Wittenberg, where they learned to replace it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is Rome's doctrine, which Skytte held and the dictionary does not excuse: he died in communion with a church teaching a repeated sacrifice of the mass, the invocation of saints, and justification by infused rather than imputed righteousness, and he resisted no part of it. The matching error is the pious reading that turns him into a secret evangelical. There is no evidence that he was. He was a conservative churchman who valued learning and underestimated what learning at Wittenberg would do.

The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the intentions of men, which neither excuses the intention nor fails of the result. Paul can rejoice in preaching done from bad motives: “whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice” (Php 1:18). Proverbs sets the human plan beside the divine direction twice over: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9), and again, “There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand” (Pro 19:21).
